questions.text:
Consider an unordered list of [latex]N [/latex] distinct integers.
What is the minimum number of element comparisons required to find an integer in the list that is NOT the largest in the list?
questions.solution:
We just need to find some element guaranteed not to be the overall largest — not identify the largest itself, and not verify anything about the rest of the list.

Compare any two elements of the list against each other: whichever of the two is smaller is guaranteed to not be the maximum of the whole list (since the larger of this pair beats it, so it can't possibly be the overall largest). This requires only one comparison, and works for any list of [latex]N\ge2[/latex] distinct integers.

Answer: 1

questions.text:
Consider a binary tree [latex]T [/latex] in which every node has either zero or two children. Let [latex]n > 0 [/latex] be the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex].
Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex] that have exactly two children?
questions.solution:
In a binary tree where every node has [latex]0[/latex] or [latex]2[/latex] children, let [latex]I[/latex] be the number of [latex]2[/latex]-children (internal) nodes and [latex]L[/latex] the number of leaves. A basic counting fact for such trees: [latex]L=I+1[/latex] (each internal node, when added, net-increases the leaf count by exactly one over what it replaced).

Total nodes: [latex]n=I+L=I+(I+1)=2I+1\ \Rightarrow\ I=\dfrac{n-1}2[/latex]

Answer: (n-1)/2

questions.text:
In a double hashing scheme, [latex] h_1(k) = k \mod 11 [/latex] and [latex] h_2(k) = 1 + (k \mod 7) [/latex] are the auxiliary hash functions. The size [latex] m [/latex] of the hash table is 11. The hash function for the [latex] i [/latex]-th probe in the open address table is [latex] [h_1(k) + i h_2(k)] \mod m [/latex] The following keys are inserted in the given order: 63, 50, 25, 79, 67, 24.

The slot at which key 24 gets stored is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.solution:
Double hashing: [latex]h_1(k)=k\bmod11[/latex], [latex]h_2(k)=1+(k\bmod7)[/latex], probe [latex]i[/latex]: [latex][h_1(k)+ih_2(k)]\bmod11[/latex], table size [latex]11[/latex].

Insert in order, computing initial slot (and probing forward on collision):
[latex]63[/latex]: [latex]h_1=8[/latex] → slot [latex]8[/latex] (empty).
[latex]50[/latex]: [latex]h_1=6[/latex] → slot [latex]6[/latex] (empty).
[latex]25[/latex]: [latex]h_1=3[/latex] → slot [latex]3[/latex] (empty).
[latex]79[/latex]: [latex]h_1=2[/latex] → slot [latex]2[/latex] (empty).
[latex]67[/latex]: [latex]h_1=1[/latex] → slot [latex]1[/latex] (empty).
[latex]24[/latex]: [latex]h_1=2[/latex] (taken by [latex]79[/latex]), [latex]h_2=1+(24\bmod7)=1+3=4[/latex]. Probe [latex]i=1[/latex]: [latex](2+4)\bmod11=6[/latex] (taken by [latex]50[/latex]). Probe [latex]i=2[/latex]: [latex](2+8)\bmod11=10[/latex] (empty) → placed at slot [latex]10[/latex].

Answer: 10

From the given lists, [latex]L1: 1,7,12,3,9,5,11,15,8[/latex] and [latex]L2:1,11,6,9,15,12,4[/latex] (so [latex]L2=\{1,11,6,9,15,12,4\}[/latex] as a lookup set).

The code walks [latex]ptr1[/latex] through [latex]L1[/latex], and for each node, looks at the next node's value: if that value is found anywhere in [latex]L2[/latex], the next node is unlinked (removed) and [latex]ptr1[/latex] stays put (to re-check the new next node); otherwise [latex]ptr1[/latex] simply advances.

Tracing through: starting value [latex]7[/latex] (not in L2) → advance. Next value [latex]12[/latex] (in L2) → delete [latex]12[/latex]. Next value [latex]3[/latex] (not in L2) → advance. Next value [latex]9[/latex] (in L2) → delete [latex]9[/latex]. Next value [latex]5[/latex] (not in L2) → advance. Next value [latex]11[/latex] (in L2) → delete [latex]11[/latex]. Next value [latex]15[/latex] (in L2) → delete [latex]15[/latex]. Next value [latex]8[/latex] (not in L2) → advance; now at the last node, loop ends.

Nodes removed: [latex]12,9,11,15[/latex] ([latex]4[/latex] nodes), leaving [latex]9-4=5[/latex] nodes: [latex]1,7,3,5,8[/latex].

Answer: 5

questions.text: The height of any rooted tree is defined as the maximum number of edges in the path from the root node to any leaf node. Suppose a Min-Heap [latex]T[/latex] stores 32 keys. The height of [latex]T[/latex] is _____________. (Answer in integer)
questions.solution:
A min-heap with [latex]N[/latex] keys is stored as a nearly-complete binary tree, and its height (max edges from root to a leaf) is [latex]\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor[/latex].

Level [latex]0[/latex] holds [latex]1[/latex] node, level [latex]1[/latex] holds [latex]2[/latex], level [latex]2[/latex] holds [latex]4[/latex], level [latex]3[/latex] holds [latex]8[/latex], level [latex]4[/latex] holds [latex]16[/latex] — cumulatively [latex]1+2+4+8+16=31[/latex] nodes fill levels [latex]0[/latex] through [latex]4[/latex] completely. The [latex]32[/latex]nd key must then start a new level, level 5.

Answer: 5
